title: The Song of the Strong City and the Dead Who Will Live
summary: Judah sings of a strong city whose walls are salvation, where the LORD keeps in perfect peace those who trust him, while the lofty city is brought down. The people confess their longing for God, their failure to bring salvation to the earth, and their hope that, unlike the dead rulers who oppressed them, God's own dead will live and rise from the dust. The chapter closes by telling God's people to hide briefly while the LORD comes out to punish the earth's wickedness.
story: Chapter 25 described the feast on Zion and the swallowing of death. Chapter 26 gives the song the redeemed will sing "in that day," and then turns into a prayer from people who are still waiting for that day to arrive. That mix of future song and present longing is the heart of the chapter. It gathers up Isaiah's steady theme of trust (compare 7:9 and 30:15) and pushes the hope of chapter 25 further, to the rising of the dead. The final verses, with the LORD coming out of his dwelling to judge, lead into the defeat of Leviathan at the start of chapter 27.
historical:
As with chapters 24 and 25, the dating of this song belongs to the wider debate over chapters 24 to 27. On the traditional view it is the prophecy of Isaiah in the late eighth or early seventh century BC, in the years when Assyria dominated Judah; on many critical views it comes from the community after the exile, in the Persian period, when Judah was small, poor, and ruled by foreign powers. Either setting fits the confession of verse 13, that "other lords besides You have had dominion" over the people. Judah was ruled or dominated in turn by Assyria, Babylon, and Persia, and the song's contrast between those foreign lords, now dead and forgotten, and the LORD whose name alone Israel confesses would have spoken to readers in any of those centuries.

The mention of verse 19, that the dead will live and their bodies will rise, has made the chapter important in the history of Jewish and Christian belief about resurrection. Scholars who date the section late sometimes argue that belief in bodily resurrection developed only after the exile; those who date it early reply that the hope has roots in older texts, such as Hannah's song that the LORD brings down to Sheol and raises up (1 Samuel 2:6).
cultural:
A walled city was the ancient world's picture of safety. Its walls and ramparts, a double line of defense, decided whether a population survived a siege. The song says that Judah's strong city has salvation itself for its walls, and its gates open not to an army but to a faithful nation. The contrast with the lofty city trampled by the feet of the poor (verses 5 and 6) turns the ancient order upside down.

Israel pictured the dead as going down to Sheol, the shadowy place of the dead, where they existed as rephaim, weak shades cut off from the life of the land. Verse 14 uses that word for the dead oppressors: they are shades who will not rise. The hope of verse 19 is set against that background. Dew was vital in a land where rain fell only in certain months; in the dry summer, heavy morning dew sustained crops. God's dew falling on the dust and bringing up the dead is a farmer's picture of new life after a long drought. The image of labor pains in verses 17 and 18 was also familiar: childbirth was the most dangerous thing most women did, and pain with no child born was a picture of complete futility.
literary: The chapter is a psalm in several movements. Verses 1 to 6 are a song of victory for the strong city. Verses 7 to 11 turn to reflection on the way of the righteous and on why the wicked do not learn. Verses 12 to 19 are a communal prayer, moving from confession of God's past help to honest lament ("we gave birth to wind") to the sudden promise of resurrection. Verses 20 and 21 are an oracle telling God's people to hide until his wrath passes. The chapter is full of deliberate pairs: the dead rulers who "will not live" in verse 14 are answered by God's dead who "will live" in verse 19; the lofty city laid in the dust in verse 5 is answered by the dwellers in the dust who awake to sing. The Hebrew of verse 3 repeats the word for peace, shalom shalom, which the BSB renders "perfect peace."

outline.t: The song of the strong city and the fall of the lofty city
Waiting for God on the level path of the righteous
Other lords have ruled, but the LORD alone is confessed
Labor without birth, and the promise that the dead will live
Hide until the wrath has passed

doctrines.note: Verses 3 and 4 tie peace to trust: God keeps the steadfast mind in perfect peace "because he trusts in You," and the people are called to trust the LORD because he is "the Rock eternal." Faith rests on the character of the one trusted.
Verse 19 promises that God's dead will live and their bodies will rise. Whatever its first readers understood, the verse became one of the Old Testament's anchors for belief in bodily resurrection.

The chapter models honest prayer: longing for God at night, confession of failure, and appeal to God's past faithfulness. The people pour out "a quiet prayer" in distress and admit that their own efforts produced nothing.

words.note: Shalom, peace. The word means wholeness and well-being, not only the absence of conflict: health, safety, right relationships, and enough. Verse 3 doubles it to express completeness, and verse 12 says that the LORD will establish shalom for his people, because everything they have accomplished he has done for them.

Batach, to trust, to feel secure. The word describes leaning one's weight on something. Isaiah uses it often, especially in the Assyrian crisis, where the question is what Judah will rely on (36:4-7). Here the object of trust is the LORD, the eternal Rock.

Rephaim, the shades or departed spirits. The same Hebrew word also names an ancient people remembered as giants (Deuteronomy 2:11), and in poetry it names the dead in Sheol. Verse 14 says of the dead oppressors that the rephaim will not rise, while verse 19 promises that the land will give birth to them, a striking reversal for God's people.

christ: The New Testament's hope of resurrection draws on texts like verse 19, though it does not quote this verse directly. Jesus said that an hour is coming when all who are in the graves will hear his voice and come out (John 5:28-29), language close to Isaiah's call to the dwellers in the dust. Paul's call to the sleeper to rise from the dead so that Christ will shine on him (Ephesians 5:14) may echo this chapter and chapter 60, though its exact source is uncertain. The people's confession in verse 18, that they could bring no salvation to the earth, is answered in the Gospels by the one who did: Jesus, the true Israel, who brought life to the world. His own resurrection on the third day is, in Paul's phrase, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Corinthians 15:20), the first of the dead to rise.

hard.q: Verse 14 says the dead will not live, and verse 19 says the dead will live. Does the chapter contradict itself?
hard.a:
The two verses speak about different groups, and the contrast is deliberate. Verse 14 describes the foreign lords who ruled Israel: they are dead, they will not rise, and their memory has been wiped out. Verse 19 speaks of "Your dead," the LORD's own people, who will live. The point is that the oppressors' power ends at the grave, while God's people have a future beyond it.

The harder question is what verse 19 meant to its first readers. Some scholars read it as a picture of national revival, like the valley of dry bones in Ezekiel 37, where Israel's return from exile is described as graves opening. Others hold that it speaks of literal bodily resurrection, and note how closely Daniel 12:2 echoes its language of those who sleep in the dust awaking. Many see both: a promise of national restoration expressed in terms that point beyond it to the resurrection of the body.

questions: Verse 3 links perfect peace with a steadfast mind that trusts God. What competes for your trust, and what would it look like to lean your weight on God instead?
The people confess that they labored and gave birth only to wind (verse 18). Where have you seen effort that produced nothing, and how does the chapter answer that experience?
How does the promise that the dead will live change the way a person faces grief, or faces powerful people who seem to have the last word?
